title: PMSM vs Induction Motor for EVs: Which Is Better? | Skill-Lync
summary: PMSM vs induction motor for EVs, worked: slip, torque-slip curve, base speed, a same-size efficiency test, Tesla's mixed setup and Indian EV motors.
body_markdown:
A permanent magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) gets its rotor field from magnets, so the rotor turns in step with the stator's rotating field and wastes almost no energy. An induction motor has no magnets: the stator field induces currents in a copper or aluminium rotor cage, which only happens if the rotor slips slightly behind the field. That makes the PMSM smaller and more efficient in everyday driving, and the induction motor cheaper, free of rare earths and able to switch its field off when idle. Every Indian EV we checked whose maker names the motor type, from the Nexon.ev to the Ather 450X, uses a PMSM. Tata's Harrier.ev QWD adds an induction motor on the second axle.


Below, both machines are worked through with numbers: synchronous speed and slip, a torque-slip curve from a textbook equivalent circuit, and P = Tω on a motor Oak Ridge National Laboratory tested. Then efficiency, cost, control, the rare-earth-free options and the Indian line-up.


## Key numbers at a glance


- **2,728 rpm:** base speed of the 2012 Nissan LEAF's 80 kW, 280 N·m interior-magnet motor, about 40 km/h in the car. Below it the motor gives full torque, above it full power up to 10,390 rpm (ORNL test data, 2013).
- **85.5% vs 83.0%:** efficiency of a Toyota Prius 2010 interior PM motor and a same-size copper-cage induction motor, both making about 221 N·m at 250 A. The induction motor's active parts were 11% heavier and 9% cheaper (Gundogdu, Zhu and Chan, 2022).
- **6%:** at 6% slip, 6% of the air-gap power of an induction motor becomes heat in the rotor: 967 W out of 16.1 kW in our textbook example.
- **Rear PMSM + front induction:** the layout of the Tesla Model 3 and Model Y (2021) and of the Tata Harrier.ev QWD (175 kW rear, 116 kW front; Tata Motors, 3 June 2025).


**Courses:** to design or control these machines, see Skill-Lync's[electric vehicle courses](https://skill-lync.com/courses/electric-vehicle) , including[Electric Motor Design using MATLAB and ANSYS Maxwell](https://skill-lync.com/electrical-engineering-courses/electric-motor-design) and[Control Theory PMSM](https://skill-lync.com/electrical-engineering-courses/control-theory-pmsm) .


## What is the difference between a PMSM and an induction motor?


Both motors have almost the same stator: laminated steel with three-phase windings fed by an inverter. The difference is the rotor. A PMSM rotor carries permanent magnets, usually neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB), and turns at exactly synchronous speed. An induction motor rotor is a steel stack with shorted copper or aluminium bars, magnetised by currents the stator induces in them.

Rotor field from Permanent magnets, always on Currents induced in the rotor cage


Rotor speed Exactly synchronous Slightly below synchronous (slip)


Rotor losses Very small Slip × air-gap power


Part-load efficiency Higher Lower; draws magnetising current even at light load


Torque per kg Higher Lower for the same size

Spinning while idle Magnets still magnetise the steel: iron loss and back-EMF No current, no field, almost no drag


Main risk Demagnetisation at high temperature and current Rotor heat, which is hard to remove


For the background theory, see the chapters on[traction motors](https://skill-lync.com/books/electric-vehicles#unit-7-motors) and[induction motor performance](https://skill-lync.com/books/electrical-machines#unit-10-induction-motor-performance) in our free textbooks.


## How does a PMSM make torque?


A PMSM makes torque because the stator's rotating field pulls on the rotor magnets, like dragging a compass needle around with a magnet. The inverter keeps the stator field about 90 electrical degrees ahead of the magnets, where the pull is strongest. Interior-magnet designs add a second, "reluctance" torque from the rotor steel.

With surface magnets, 300 A gives at most 144 N·m, at 0°. With interior magnets, the same magnet flux and current give up to 195 N·m at 31.3°, 35% more, and 37% of it is reluctance torque. That best angle is the **maximum torque per ampere (MTPA)** point, and tracking it is the controller's job. This is why well-documented car PMSMs, such as the Prius 2010 and LEAF motors, are interior-magnet designs.


## How does an induction motor make torque?


The rotating stator field sweeps past the rotor bars and induces currents in them. Those currents make their own field, which the stator field drags along. Induction needs relative motion, so the rotor always turns a little slower than the field. That difference, the slip, sets both rotor current and torque.

Read the 60 Hz curve from the right. Torque is zero at synchronous speed (1,800 rpm) and rises almost in proportion to slip: 51.0 N·m at 3%, 85.5 N·m at 6%. A grid-fed motor is stuck on that one curve; an inverter-fed EV motor is not. Lowering the frequency at constant volts per hertz slides the curve left, so the motor stays on the steep part at any road speed. The 20 Hz and 40 Hz peaks are lower (74.3 and 102.7 N·m) because stator resistance matters more at low voltage, which is why drives add a "low-speed boost". The[electrical drives textbook](https://skill-lync.com/books/electrical-drives#unit-25-pmsm) covers V/f, vector control and PMSM drives.

### What is field weakening, and why do the two motors do it differently?


Field weakening means reducing the motor's effective flux so its back-EMF, the voltage the spinning motor generates against its supply, stays below the battery voltage as speed rises. Without it, the inverter runs out of voltage at base speed.


- **PMSM:** the magnet flux cannot be switched off, so the controller injects negative d-axis current to oppose it. That current makes no useful torque but still heats the copper. Interior magnets help, because reluctance torque keeps working at high speed.
- **Induction motor:** the flux comes from the magnetising current, so the controller simply asks for less. Raising frequency at the voltage limit lowers the flux on its own.


Our[EV range calculator](https://skill-lync.com/tools/ev-range-calculator) shows how much of a drive cycle such as the MIDC is spent at low speed and part load. That is where the efficiency contest below is decided.


## Which is more efficient: PMSM or induction motor?


A PMSM is more efficient at the low and medium speeds and part loads of city driving, by 2.5 percentage points in the same-size study below. It has no slip loss and draws no magnetising current. An induction motor narrows the gap at high speed and light load, where it can cut its flux while a PMSM's magnets keep magnetising the steel.


Gundogdu, Zhu and Chan (2022) took the Toyota Prius 2010 interior-magnet motor and designed a copper-cage induction motor with the same stator diameter (264 mm), stack length (50.8 mm), current (250 A peak) and voltage limit:


Same-size machine Torque Output Efficiency Losses Active mass Material cost


Interior PM (NdFeB) 222.4 N·m 34.9 kW at 1,500 rpm 85.5% 5.91 kW 22.7 kg £76.70


Copper-cage induction 220.8 N·m 33.5 kW at 1,450 rpm 83.0% 6.87 kW 25.2 kg £69.71


Source: *World Electric Vehicle Journal* 13, 137 (2022), Table 3; losses worked from output and efficiency by our script. One operating point at full current, not a drive-cycle average.


At equal torque the induction motor loses 16% more energy, much of it in the rotor bars, which the authors call the induction motor's "major disadvantage". They also found that below rated current the IPM makes more torque, while above it the induction motor's torque rises faster. The PMSM is stronger at the part loads where cars spend most of their time.


The other side is in a 2021 Chalmers University report by Mikael Alatalo. Magnet-free machines "have the possibility to lower the flux density in the motors at not so demanding operating points", which matters when a powerful motor is lightly used. In his simulations, pairing a PM motor with a magnet-free reluctance machine halved the WLTP-cycle losses compared with two PM machines. That is the logic behind the Tesla layout.


## Why does Tesla use an induction motor on one axle?


Tesla's dual-motor Model 3 and Model Y pair an efficient permanent magnet motor on the rear axle with an induction motor on the front (Gundogdu et al., 2022; Chalmers, 2021). An induction motor with no current has no field, so it can spin almost freely while the PM motor cruises, then join in for acceleration or grip.


- **Early cars:** Tesla's first models used AC induction motors; the Model 3 introduced its permanent magnet motor (Electrek, reporting Tesla's Investor Day, 1 March 2023).
- **Model S and X update, 23 April 2019:** a permanent magnet motor moved to the front, and the rear induction motor "engages when extra power is needed". Engadget reported the Long Range Model S's EPA range rising from 335 to 370 miles.
- **Model 3 and Model Y, 2021:** induction front, interior PM rear ( *World Electric Vehicle Journal* , 2022, Table 1).


tesla.com refused automated access and we found no Tesla technical paper giving its reasoning, so treat the free-spinning explanation as engineering logic, not a company statement.


India now has the same layout. Tata's release for the Harrier.ev QWD (3 June 2025) gives 238 PS (175 kW) and 158 PS (116 kW) from its two motors and 504 N·m combined. A review on the Tata Group newsroom describes the rear unit as a permanent magnet synchronous motor and the front as an induction motor. Rear-wheel-drive variants use the PMSM alone.


## Power density, cost and magnets: what does each motor trade?


A PMSM gives more torque per kilogram but needs NdFeB magnets. An induction motor uses cheaper copper, aluminium and steel but is heavier for the same output. In the same-size study, the induction motor's active parts were 11.1% heavier and 9.1% cheaper.


- **Specific torque:** 9.80 N·m per kg of active material for the IPM, 8.75 for the copper-cage motor.
- **Whole motor:** the LEAF motor, about 56 kg and 19 litres for 80 kW, gives 1.43 kW/kg and 4.2 kW/L (ORNL), housing and cooling included.
- **Materials:** the study priced NdFeB at £42.28/kg, copper at £7.354/kg and electrical steel at £0.44/kg. A kilogram of magnet costs as much as nearly 6 kg of copper.


Supply is the bigger exposure: NdFeB depends heavily on China, and the heat-resistant grades on dysprosium or terbium. The 2025 export controls, India's ₹


7,280 crore magnet scheme and how much magnet a motor holds are in[Rare Earth Magnet Shortage: What It Means for EV Motors in India](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/rare-earth-magnet-shortage-ev-motors-india) .


## What limits each motor: heat and demagnetisation


A PMSM is limited by its magnets. NdFeB loses coercivity, its resistance to demagnetisation, as it heats up. A hot magnet facing a strong opposing stator field, in hard acceleration or a fault, can lose strength for good; Gundogdu et al. found the IPM's demagnetisation risk rising with current. Designers cap peak current, cool the rotor and pick high-temperature grades, which brings back the dysprosium question.


An induction motor is limited by rotor heat. Its rotor losses (967 W at 6% slip in our 20 hp example) arise in a spinning part that is hard to cool. But there are no magnets to damage, and the same study cites earlier work crediting induction motors with better overload capability. That suits an axle that works hard for a few seconds at a time.


One more PMSM property: its magnets generate back-EMF whenever the rotor turns, even with the inverter off. At high speed that voltage can exceed the battery voltage, so the drive must handle a sudden loss of field-weakening current. An unexcited induction motor generates nothing.


## How are EV motors controlled? Field-oriented control in one paragraph


Both motors use **field-oriented control (FOC)** , or vector control. The controller measures the phase currents and uses the Clarke and Park transforms to turn them into two steady values in a frame that rotates with the rotor field:


i


d


​


, which makes flux, and


i


q


​


, which makes torque. Two PI regulators hold them at their targets, inverse transforms give the voltage commands, and space-vector PWM switches the inverter. Texas Instruments' application note BPRA073 (1998) describes this as giving an AC motor the easy control of a DC machine. A PMSM controller reads rotor angle from a resolver, encoder or observer and picks


i


d


​


for MTPA or field weakening. An induction motor's rotor-flux angle cannot be measured directly, so the controller estimates it, typically from the commanded slip, and that estimate depends on a rotor resistance that changes as the rotor heats. The cascaded speed and current loops are the same ones you can try on a DC motor in our[DC motor speed control calculator](https://skill-lync.com/tools/dc-motor-speed-control-calculator) .


## What about rare-earth-free options: switched reluctance and wound-rotor motors?


Besides the induction motor, two magnet-free designs matter. The wound-rotor synchronous motor (also called EESM, electrically excited synchronous motor) is in production. The switched reluctance motor (SRM) is still mostly in research for cars.


- **Wound rotor (EESM):** a DC-fed copper field winding replaces the magnets, so it works like a PMSM whose "magnet" the controller can turn down. Renault has used it since the Kangoo Z.E. in 2011, and the Renault 5 uses the 110 kW 6AK motor; Renault says such motors are "slightly bigger" than PM motors (16 October 2025). BMW says the iX3's 210 kW motor, built from 2020, "eliminates the need for rare earth materials". The costs are rotor copper loss and transferring power to a spinning rotor.
- **Switched reluctance (SRM):** plain toothed steel rotor, no windings, no magnets, pulled from pole to pole as stator coils switch in turn. Rugged and cheap, but its torque ripple is "severely pronounced", so it is noisy, and it needs its own converter instead of a standard three-phase inverter (Abdel-Aziz et al., *Energies* , 2024).


Ferrite magnets and reduced-dysprosium NdFeB keep the PMSM layout but change the magnet; see our[rare earth magnet explainer](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/rare-earth-magnet-shortage-ev-motors-india) .


## Which motor do Indian EVs use?


Every mainstream Indian EV in our check whose maker publishes a motor type uses a PMSM, with the Harrier.ev QWD adding a front induction motor. The table lists only what each manufacturer's own sheet or page states.

Mahindra's INGLO page gives 210 kW and 380 N·m but, like the BE 6 specification brochure we opened, does not name the motor type, so Mahindra is not listed. Scooter makers have also changed magnet grades since 2025 (Ather's heavy-rare-earth-free motor, Ola's ferrite motor), so "PMSM" alone does not tell you which magnet is inside.


## PMSM or induction motor: which should an EV use?


Use an interior-magnet PMSM as the main drive motor when efficiency, range and size matter most, which covers most cars and nearly all two-wheelers. Consider an induction or wound-rotor motor for a second axle that idles most of the time, for high power used briefly, or when magnet cost and supply risk outweigh a few points of efficiency. Performance AWD cars often do both, as Tesla and the Harrier.ev QWD show.


The limits of this article: the efficiency figures come from one same-size study at one load point and one simulation report, and real motors are optimised differently. The IPM figure uses illustrative, unsaturated parameters, and the induction curve is a 20 hp textbook machine, not a traction motor. Use the worked numbers to understand the behaviour, and finite-element analysis and test data to choose a motor.


To go further, Skill-Lync's[EV Powertrain: Component Sizing and Specification](https://skill-lync.com/electrical-engineering-courses/ev-powertrain-component-sizing-specification) course sizes a motor against a vehicle and drive cycle. Our posts on[power converters in EVs](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/power-converters-in-electric-vehicle-and-hybrid-electric-vehicle) and the[single-phase induction motor](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/history-of-single-phase-induction-motor-its-construction-working-principle-and-types) cover the inverter side and the household cousin of the traction motor.


## Frequently asked questions


### Is a BLDC motor the same as a PMSM?


They are built almost the same way, with magnets on the rotor and windings on the stator, but driven differently. A BLDC motor has a trapezoidal back-EMF and is driven with six-step switching from Hall sensors. A PMSM has a sinusoidal back-EMF and is driven with sinusoidal currents under field-oriented control. Our[BLDC drives chapter](https://skill-lync.com/books/electrical-drives#unit-26-bldc) walks through six-step commutation.


### What is the slip of an induction motor in an EV?


Usually a few percent at normal load, because the inverter keeps the motor on the steep, low-slip part of its torque curve. In our textbook example, full-load slip is 6% and pull-out comes at 14.7%. Rotor copper loss equals slip times air-gap power, so lower slip means a cooler rotor.


### What is base speed in an EV motor?


It is the speed at which the motor reaches full power while still at full torque. Below it torque is constant; above it power is constant and torque falls with speed. For the 2012 Nissan LEAF motor, 80 kW and 280 N·m give 2,728 rpm, about 40 km/h in that car.


### Do electric scooters in India use PMSM or BLDC motors?


The makers' own sheets say PMSM or IPM for the scooters we checked: the Ather 450X lists a 6.4 kW PMSM and Ola lists a mid-drive IPM for the S1 X. Some budget scooters advertise "BLDC hub motors". The label tells you more about how the motor is driven than how it is built.
